title: Personal Pronouns
objectives: understand English pronouns and their various uses
learn and translate the various Greek pronouns
recognize proclitics and enclitics and how they effect accent changes
describe how the pronoun works with its antecedent
describe how a pronoun is used for emphasis, possession, and in attributive and predicate positions
master 10 more high frequency vocabulary words

content.text: A pronoun is a word that stands in place of a noun usually for brevity or to avoid repetition. The person or object to which the pronoun refers is called its "antecedent."

Zach threw the ball to Elliott.
[[u]]It[[/u]] (the ball) hit [[u]]him[[/u]] (Elliott) in the head.
There are various types of Pronouns:

items.label: Personal pronouns:
items.text: stand in for a person—"Bill did it. [[u]]He[[/u]] was there."

items.label: Demonstrative pronouns:
items.text: point to a person or object which is near (this/these) or far (that/those).

items.label: Relative pronouns:
items.text: relate a subordinate clause to a noun—"It is a great person [[u]]who[[/u]] attempts to master Greek."

items.label: Reciprocal pronouns:
items.text: state an interchange between two things/persons—They loved [[u]]one another[[/u]].

items.label: Reflexive pronouns:
items.text: direct the action of the verb back to the subject—"She hid [[u]]herself[[/u]] behind the door."

items.label: Interrogative pronouns:
items.text: ask a question—[[u]]Who[[/u]] broke the chair?

content.text: In English, pronouns have three cases:

items.label: Subjective
items.text: —which are used when a pronoun is the subject of a sentence ([[u]]He[[/u]] turned left).

items.label: Possessive
items.text: —which are used to indicate ownership (He gave [[u]]his[[/u]] best).

items.label: Objective
items.text: —which are used when a pronoun is the object of a sentence (He left [[u]]him[[/u]]).

content.text: In English there are singular and plural pronouns. Pronouns agree with their antecedents in number and person.
Personal pronouns in Greek will match their antecedent in person, gender, and number. The case will be determined by the role the pronoun plays in the sentence.
Personal pronouns will be either first person (I, we), second person (you), or third person (he/she/it/they).
Greek will use the genitive where we would normally use a possessive pronoun (e.g. his, her).
Since the nominative is indicated in the personal ending of the verb (e.g. λέγω = I say) when the personal pronoun is used it is for emphasis (e.g. ἐγὼ λέγω = [[u]]I[[/u]] say).
In the first and second person there are emphatic forms. These are usually the forms used in prepositional phrases.

content.title: First Person Paradigm
content.note: Emphatic first person forms are made by prefixing an epsilon and adding an accent to the genitive, dative and accusative singular forms ( ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ).

content.title: Second Person Paradigm
content.note: The emphatic form is made by adding an accent to the singulars ( σοῦ, σοί, σέ ).

content.text: An enclitic is a word that is phonetically attached so closely with the word that precedes it that it has no accent of its own. Many personal pronouns are enclitics (e.g. μου, μοι, με, σου, σοι, σε).

items: when the first word in a sentence.

content.text: If the preceding word has an acute on the antepenult or a circumflex on the penult, a second accent will be added on the ultima. This results in the word preceding the enclitic being double accented.
Finally, an acute on the ultima is not changed to a grave before an enclitic.

The third person pronoun αὐτός differs from the first and second person pronouns in that it is marked for gender. With first and second person pronouns, there is no need to specify gender because it is understood as the one speaking or one being spoken to.
αὐτός also has some other special features which we will examine here.

topics.title: Three Uses

content.text: αὐτός can be used in three ways:

items.text: [[u]]As a pronoun[[/u]]—matching its antecedent in number and gender and translated as "he," "she," "it," or "they."

examples.gloss: in three days I will raise it

items.text: [[u]]Reflexive Intensifier[[/u]]—when it is used as an adjective in the predicate position (usually in the nominative case) it is translated reflexively (e.g. he [[u]]himself[[/u]] will get the car).
[[u]]Adjective meaning "same"[[/u]]—when it is used as an adjective in the attributive position, it is translated as "same."
